“Snug but movable, same clearance nurse bees give queen larvae—just room to vibrate for temperature checks.”  

“Vibrate? I don’t want the branch vibrating, I want it set.”  

“Static is fine; I meant bees use vibration to communicate distance via the waggle dance—your wire should stay still.”  

He eyed the brown band already forming beneath the coil. “Okay, focus check—if the cambium browns overnight, do I unwind immediately?”  

“Yes, unwind fast; hives react quickly to overheating by fanning wings, and you should react the same to pressure marks.”

Gul hunched over a six-inch square of storm-scavenged roofing tin, sleeves rolled high, black fingerprints mapping where the metal had bitten back. Across the vinyl snowflakes, Hristo cradled a leaking reindeer mug like it might spill state secrets. Arm hair gone silver, forearms laddered with pale scars—each mark a quiet résumé of forty years talking sheet stock into behaving.

Gul didn’t do small talk. “I want it to catch light like a mirror, but every time I fold the edges it stays sharp enough to draw blood. How do I fix that without making it dull?”

Hristo didn’t look up. “You’re folding once and leaving it. Double fold, quarter inch in, then push the seam flat with the flat face of the hammer. Cuts the edge, hides the burr.”

Gul’s eyebrow ticked—one impatient metronome beat. “Won’t that eat the crisp line? I’m chasing a snowflake—details less than an eighth.”

For the first time, Hristo smiled, small, like a man discovering he liked the song on the radio. “Crisp line stays if you score first. Ball-peen to mark the inside score, then bend on the score with needle-nose pliers. Metal follows the rule rather than your thumbs guessing.” He demonstrated with invisible tools, wrists loose, muscle memory humming.

Gul tilted the tin, checking angles only calculus majors worried about. “What about reflection? Folded edge blocks half the angle.”

“Fold’s on the back. Front face stays flat.” Hristo tapped the table twice for emphasis. “320-grit sponge after the fold, light circles, six passes—takes the micro-burr and polishes.”

Any trick for the back without hiding the hammer texture? Gul’s voice pared down to just the words necessary.

“Skip the sponge on texture zones.” Hristo reached for a roll of blue painter’s tape, tore a sliver absent-mindedly precise. “Mask painter’s tape cut to silhouette, polish around it, peel after.”

The roll went back, its end fluttered like surrender. Gul’s fingers drummed. “How long does the sponge last before it clogs?”

“These tins shred cheap sponge in ten ornaments.” He shrugged, the kind of shrug that had once reset radial-arm saws. “Rinse under hot tap, thumb rub, dries in two minutes, good as new.”

Gul nodded once, economical. “Easy enough. Thanks—figured I’d have to grind.”

Hristo lifted the reindeer mug in a motion too smooth to be toast and too definite to be dismissal. “Grinding eats tin thickness faster than rust. Keep the hammer singing, tin behaves.”

The guy paused, hand resting on a short walnut off-cut destined for nobody's project. "Cut it a hair wide, then wax the tongue. Expansion leaves breathing room."

He slid a business card between two stacked off-cuts. "Slip a playing card through; if it drags, hit it once more with the plane."

"Ends first, long grain last. Clamps every four inches; cherry forgives if you rush."

She exhaled. The caliper went back on its hook. "Price check—twenty bucks cover it?"

She rattled her notes. “Twenty-eight by eight. Window on the door, a tri-fold exam bench, one small fridge.”

He wiped his hands on a rag that couldn’t get dirtier. “Start with envelope—walls, roof, floor. R-13 typical here, so U-value’s about point-oh-seven-seven per square foot.”

Her pen hovered. “Already lost me. Can you say BTUs?”

“Fair. Surface area around eight-twenty square feet inside the shell; delta-T we use thirty degrees—outside forty-five, inside a pleasant seventy-five. 820 times .077 times 30 gives one-nine-hundred BTU.”

“That’s just the shell?”

“Just thermal conduction. Then add infiltration—cheap door gasket, say one air change per hour, adds another eight hundred BTU roughly.”

She scribbled. “So we’re at twenty-seven hundred.”

“Plus. The fridge pulls two-fifty watts running, another eight-fifty BTU.”

“Thirty-five fifty—does lighting count?”

“Six T8 LED tubes at thirty-five watts each; tack on two-hundred extra, barely hurts.”

Sameer slid a jack-stand aside; the clang echoed. Jolene shifted weight from one frozen foot to the other. “People is the variable, right?”

“Yep. Two staff plus one patient at five-hundred BTU sensible load per body: fifteen hundred BTU, spikes to twenty-two fifty while stressed patient is inside.”

“And solar load, sun hitting the thing?”

Sameer squinted at the unpainted aluminum roof, already blinding under low sun. “Solar depends on which wall faces south, color, and shade. Unpainted aluminum roof like this gets nuked. We call it three-hundred BTU per square foot roof peak at noon—roof area two-twenty—sixty-six hundred BTU baked in.”

“Crud. That kicks us past ten grand BTU installed.”

He offered a half-smile; the calculator in his head had already rounded. “Smallest mini-split that meets FDA clean-room spec is twelve thousand. Gives you buffer for a heatwave and a full waiting line.”

“So fifteen percent fudge factor is sane?”

“Fifteen is generous. Grab the twelve K motor and sleep easy.”

The clipboard finally stopped trembling. Jolene tore the top sheet, folded the numbers into her pocket like contraband, and headed for the warm office glow, the diesel wind pushing at her back. Behind her Sameer ducked under the ribs of the bus again, tools clinking comfort against the ticking welds.
